intro: The first skateboards were planks of wood with metal roller-skate wheels nailed on. Surfers in California rode them on sidewalks when the ocean was flat. By the mid-1960s, companies sold boards in stores, and a national contest was on TV. Then the craze faded, because the wheels slipped, jammed and threw riders off.

In the 1970s, a new wheel made of urethane changed everything. It gripped the ground and rolled over cracks. A kicktail let riders lift the nose. Smooth bearings spun longer. A team from Santa Monica brought a low surf style, and empty pools in a drought gave skaters curved walls to ride.

In this unit you will meet the people, places and inventions of skateboarding's first two booms. You will learn why a hard wheel stops at a pebble and why a soft one rolls on. You will practice a tail press safely. You will see how energy changes on a curved wall.
bigQuestion: How did better wheels and new places to ride turn a fading fad into a lasting sport?

title: From Clay Wheels to Urethane

chapters.title: The First Boom
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a homemade toy become a craze across America, and why did that craze fade so fast?

story.title: Stopped by a Pebble
story.kicker: A girl rolls down a California sidewalk in 1964, and one tiny stone ends her ride.
paragraphs: It is a warm afternoon in a California beach town in 1964. Ruth stands on her new board. It is a short wooden plank. Under it are four metal wheels from an old pair of roller skates. The ocean is flat today, so there are no waves to surf.

Ruth pushes off. The steel wheels clatter and buzz on the sidewalk. She can feel every crack through her feet. She bends her knees and leans a little, the way she leans on a surfboard. The board curves gently to one side.

Then the front wheel hits a tiny pebble. The hard metal wheel cannot roll over it. The board stops dead. Ruth does not stop. Her body keeps moving forward, and she tumbles onto the grass beside the sidewalk.
Ruth sits up and checks her hands. They are scraped, but she is fine. She looks back at the pebble. It is smaller than a pea. "How can something so small stop a whole board?" she wonders.

Thousands of riders in the 1960s asked the same question. The boards of that time were fun, but their wheels were rough and slippery. It would take years, and a brand-new kind of wheel, to fix the problem.
story.think: Why did the board stop at the pebble while Ruth kept moving forward?

lessons.title: Surfing on the Sidewalk
lessons.mainIdea: In California in the late 1950s, surfers rode boards on sidewalks when the ocean had no good waves.
reading: In the late 1950s, many young people in California loved to surf. But the ocean does not always make good waves. Some days the water is flat. Surfers wanted a way to keep riding on those days.

So they rode on land. They stood on small boards with wheels and rolled down sidewalks and gentle streets. They bent their knees and leaned to turn, just like on a wave. People called this *sidewalk surfing*.

Sidewalk surfing spread along the beach towns of California in the late 1950s and early 1960s. The riders were not doing flips or jumps. They carved smooth curves and copied surf moves. The *skateboard* had begun as a way to surf without water.

words.d: an early name for skateboarding, when surfers rode boards on sidewalks like waves
a board with wheels underneath that a person stands on and rides

lessons.title: Making a Board at Home
lessons.mainIdea: The first skateboards were homemade: a wooden plank with roller-skate wheels fastened underneath.
reading: The first skateboards were not bought in stores. Kids made them at home. They took an old pair of metal *roller skates* and pulled them apart. Each skate had a front set of wheels and a back set.
Next, they fastened the wheel sets under a plank of wood. Some used nails. Some used screws. A short piece of a two-by-four board worked. So did a wooden crate or a piece of old furniture.
These homemade boards were stiff and flat. They had no curved tail. The wheels were small and made of metal. But they rolled, and kids could ride them. That was enough to start something new.

words.d: shoes or frames with wheels under them; early riders took their wheels to build skateboards

lessons.title: Who Made the First One?
lessons.mainIdea: No one person is known to have invented the skateboard; many people built them in many places.
reading: People love to ask who invented the skateboard. You may hear a story about one boy or one town. These are stories. No record shows a single first inventor.

Historians look for proof, like dated photos, ads and newspaper stories. For the first skateboards, there is very little. Kids built boards in garages and did not write it down. Many people likely had the same idea in different places.

So the honest answer is that we do not know. What we do know is where the idea grew. It grew among surfers and kids in California in the late 1950s. A *historian* says what the proof shows, and says when the proof runs out.

words.d: a person who studies the past using proof such as records, photos and objects
something written, printed or photographed that shows what happened

look.text: Two people tell you about the first skateboard. The first says, "My uncle made the very first one in 1955." The second shows a dated photo of kids riding plank boards in a California town in 1959. Only one of them has proof you can check.
look.prompt: Which claim would a historian trust more, and why?

check.why: No record shows one inventor; many people built boards in many places.

choices: dated photos, ads and newspaper stories
check.why: Historians trust records such as dated photos, ads and newspaper stories.

sections.title: Boards in Stores, Wheels That Slip

lessons.title: Store Boards Arrive
lessons.mainIdea: Around 1959 stores began selling skateboards, and by the early 1960s companies like Makaha and Hobie were making them.
reading: Around 1959, the first skateboards made by companies showed up in stores. Now a kid did not need a hammer and an old skate. A family could just buy a board.

In 1963, a surfer named Larry Stevenson started a company called *Makaha*. It made skateboards. In the 1960s, boards also carried the Hobie name, from the surfboard maker Hobie Alter. Surf companies knew their riders wanted to skate.

Store boards were shaped better than planks. Their wheels were held by metal parts called *trucks*. Trucks hold the wheels and let the board turn when the rider leans. Early trucks came from roller skates, too.

words.d: an early skateboard company started by surfer Larry Stevenson in 1963
the metal parts under the deck that hold the wheels and let the board turn

lessons.title: Clay Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: Many 1960s boards rolled on clay wheels, which were quieter than metal but slid out easily.
reading: By the mid-1960s, many store boards rolled on *clay wheels*. They were not made of plain clay from the ground. They were a hard, pressed mix of materials. People called them clay because they looked and felt like it.

Clay wheels were quieter than metal wheels. They felt a little smoother on a sidewalk. But they had a big problem. They did not grip the ground well. On a turn, a clay wheel could slide sideways and throw the rider off.
Clay wheels also wore down fast. They chipped on rough concrete. A rider might need new wheels often. These wheels were better than steel, but not by much.

words.d: hard wheels made of a pressed mix of materials, used on many 1960s skateboards
how well something holds onto a surface instead of sliding

look.title: A Turn on Clay
look.text: Picture a rider on clay wheels leaning into a sharp turn. The board curves for a moment. Then the wheels skid sideways across the concrete with a scraping sound. The board shoots out to the side, and the rider steps off fast.
look.prompt: What did the clay wheels fail to do during the turn?

check.q: What were clay wheels really made of?

check.q: What was the biggest problem with clay wheels?

check.why: Clay wheels were quieter and a little smoother than metal wheels.

lessons.title: Steel Wheels and Noise
lessons.mainIdea: Steel wheels were loud, shaky and slippery, and they jammed at even a tiny stone.
reading: The earliest boards rolled on *steel wheels* from roller skates. Steel is a hard metal. It does not squish at all. On a sidewalk, steel wheels made a loud clattering, buzzing sound.
Because steel is so hard, every bump went right into the rider's feet. Riders felt each crack in the concrete. The board shook and rattled. On smooth, slick ground, steel wheels also slid easily.

The worst problem was small stones. A hard wheel cannot squeeze around a pebble. It hits the pebble and *jams*. The board stops in an instant, and the rider is thrown forward. Riders had to watch for tiny stones all the time.

words.d: hard metal wheels from roller skates, used on the earliest skateboards
to get stuck so it cannot move or turn

look.text: Picture a steel wheel rolling toward a pebble the size of a pea. The wheel is hard, so it does not bend. It bumps the front of the pebble. Instead of rolling up and over, it jams. The whole board stops in one instant.
look.prompt: What would need to change about the wheel so it could roll over the pebble?

check.why: Hard steel wheels clattered and buzzed loudly on concrete.

check.q: Why did riders feel every crack on steel wheels?
choices: Steel is hard and does not squish.
check.why: Steel does not squish, so every bump went straight into the rider's feet.

check.q: What happens when a steel wheel hits a small pebble?
choices: It rolls up and over easily.

check.why: A hard wheel cannot squeeze around a pebble, so it jams and the board stops.

lessons.title: Why the Rider Keeps Going
lessons.mainIdea: When a board stops suddenly, the rider's body keeps moving forward until something stops it.
reading: Think about Ruth and the pebble. The board stopped, but Ruth flew forward. Why? A moving body keeps moving. It keeps going the same way until something pushes or pulls on it.

The pebble pushed back on the wheel. That stopped the board. But nothing pushed back on Ruth's body. Her feet were only resting on the deck. So she kept going forward and fell off. This is called *inertia*.

You feel inertia in a car, too. When the car stops fast, your body leans forward. A seat belt is what stops you. Skaters learn to bend their knees and watch the ground ahead. That helps them catch their balance or step off safely.

words.d: the way a moving thing keeps moving, or a still thing stays still, until a push or pull changes it
the flat board a skater stands on

sections.title: Champions on TV, Then a Crash

reading: In 1965, the first *National Skateboard Championships* took place in Anaheim, California. Riders came to compete in front of a crowd. It was a big step. Skating was becoming a sport, not only a toy.

The contest was shown on ABC's Wide World of Sports. That was a popular TV show about many sports. Families all over the country watched skaters on their TV screens. Many kids saw skateboarding for the first time.
Contests of the 1960s had events like *slalom* and freestyle. In slalom, riders weave around a line of cones. In freestyle, riders show tricks on flat ground, like spins and handstands on the board.

reading: *Patti McGee* was one of the best riders of the 1960s. In 1965, she won the women's national championship. Women and girls were skating from the very start, and Patti showed how good they could be.

That same year, Patti McGee was on the cover of *Life magazine*. Life was one of the most-read magazines in America. Its covers showed big news and famous people. A skater on the cover told the whole country that skating mattered.
Patti was known for freestyle tricks, like handstands on a rolling board. She also traveled to show skating to new crowds. Many girls who saw her picture decided they could skate too.

lessons.title: The Boom Fades
lessons.mainIdea: Around 1965 to 1966 the first boom faded, as many riders got hurt on boards with poor wheels.
reading: In the early 1960s, huge numbers of skateboards were sold. People called this the first *boom*. A boom is a time when something grows very fast. Then, around 1965 and 1966, the boom faded almost as fast as it came.

One big reason was injuries. Clay and steel wheels slipped and stopped short. Many riders fell and got hurt. Few people wore helmets or pads back then. Some towns made rules against skating on streets and sidewalks.
Soon many kids put their boards away. Stores were left with boards no one bought. Skating did not disappear, but it got very small. A better wheel would bring it back in the 1970s.

chapters.title: A New Wheel Changes Everything
chapters.bigQuestion: How did one new wheel, a curved tail and empty swimming pools bring skateboarding back to life?

story.title: Over the Crack
story.kicker: In 1975 a skater rolls over a crack that used to throw riders off, and keeps on going.
paragraphs: It is 1975 on a sidewalk in Southern California. Marcus has ridden here for years. He knows every crack. There is one big crack near the corner. On his old clay wheels, that crack always made the board jerk and slide.
Today his board has new wheels. They are bright and a little soft, like a hard pencil eraser. They are made of a plastic called urethane. His older cousin bought them at a surf shop.

Marcus pushes off. The new wheels roll quietly. He can hardly hear them. He reaches the big crack and gets ready for a jolt. But the wheels squeeze over it with a soft bump, and the board keeps rolling.
He leans into a turn. On clay wheels, the board would skid sideways here. Now the wheels hold on to the concrete. The board carves a smooth curve, like a surfboard on a wave.
Marcus laughs and rides back to the corner to try again. All over California, other riders are finding the same thing. Skateboarding, which had nearly faded away, is about to boom again.
story.think: What two things did the new wheels do better than the old clay wheels?

lessons.title: Frank Nasworthy's Idea
lessons.mainIdea: In the early 1970s, Frank Nasworthy put urethane wheels on skateboards and sold them as Cadillac Wheels.
reading: In the early 1970s, a young surfer named *Frank Nasworthy* saw a new kind of roller-skate wheel. It was made of a plastic called urethane. He wondered how it would feel on a skateboard.

He tried urethane wheels on his board. They rolled smoothly and gripped the ground. They were much better than clay. Nasworthy started a company to sell them to skaters. He named it *Cadillac Wheels*, after a smooth-riding car.

Skaters who tried the wheels did not want to go back. Word spread from rider to rider and shop to shop. By the mid-1970s, urethane wheels were everywhere. They helped start skateboarding's second boom.

words.d: the surfer who brought urethane wheels to skateboarding in the early 1970s
Frank Nasworthy's company, which sold urethane skateboard wheels in the early 1970s

look.title: Two Wheels in Your Hand
look.text: Picture holding two skateboard wheels. The clay wheel is hard and gritty. When you press it with your thumb, nothing happens. The urethane wheel is smooth. When you press hard with your thumb, it gives just a tiny bit, then springs back.
look.prompt: Which wheel would roll over a small crack more easily, and why?

check.q: Who brought urethane wheels to skateboarding in the early 1970s?
check.why: Frank Nasworthy tried urethane wheels on a skateboard and started Cadillac Wheels.

check.q: What did Frank Nasworthy name his wheel company?

check.q: What did urethane wheels help start?
check.why: Urethane wheels spread fast in the mid-1970s and helped start the second boom.

lessons.title: Why Urethane Grips
lessons.mainIdea: Urethane wheels squish a little and grip the ground, so they roll over bumps and hold on in turns.
reading: *Urethane* is a tough plastic that can bend a little and spring back. It is used for many things, like shoe soles and roller-skate wheels. On a skateboard, that small bit of give makes a big difference.

When a urethane wheel rolls onto a pebble or crack, it squishes around it for a moment. Then it springs back into shape. So the wheel rolls over small bumps instead of jamming. The ride feels smooth and quiet.

Urethane also has good *friction* with concrete. Friction is a force that pushes against sliding. When you lean into a turn, friction holds the wheels in place. The board curves instead of skidding out.

words.d: a tough plastic that bends a little and springs back; used for modern skateboard wheels
a force between two surfaces that pushes against sliding

look.title: Rub Your Hands
look.text: Rub your dry hands together fast. They get warm, and you can feel them pull on each other. That pull is friction. Now picture a wheel leaning into a turn. Friction between the wheel and the ground pulls the same way, keeping the wheel from sliding out sideways.
look.prompt: Would there be more friction on dry concrete or on wet, slick tile? Explain.

check.q: What is urethane?
choices: a tough plastic that bends a little and springs back
check.why: Urethane is a tough plastic with a little give, used for skateboard wheels.

check.q: Why does a urethane wheel roll over a small pebble?
choices: It squishes around the pebble, then springs back.
It is heavier than the pebble.
check.why: The wheel's small give lets it squish around the pebble instead of jamming.

check.q: What does friction do when a skater leans into a turn?
choices: holds the wheels so they do not slide out
check.why: Friction pushes against sliding, so the wheels hold the ground in a turn.

lessons.title: Soft and Hard Wheels
lessons.mainIdea: Wheel hardness is measured on the durometer A scale, from about 78A for soft wheels to about 101A for hard ones.
reading: Not all urethane wheels feel the same. Some are softer and some are harder. Skaters measure this with the *durometer* scale. A durometer is a tool that presses into a material to test how hard it is.
Skateboard wheels use the A scale. The number is followed by the letter A. Soft wheels are about 78A. Very hard wheels are about 101A. A bigger number means a harder wheel.

Soft wheels squish more. They roll over cracks and rough ground well and grip strongly. Hard wheels squish less. They feel fast on smooth ground and slide more easily. Skaters pick the hardness that fits where they ride.

words.d: a tool and a number scale that measure how hard a material is
how much a material resists being pressed in or squished

check.why: A durometer measures hardness by pressing into a material.

lessons.title: The Kicktail
lessons.mainIdea: Larry Stevenson's kicktail, patented in 1971, let riders press the tail to lift the front of the board.
reading: Early boards were flat from end to end. Then came the *kicktail*. A kicktail is a back end that bends upward. Larry Stevenson, who started Makaha, got a patent for it. The patent was granted in 1971.

With a kicktail, a rider can step on the *tail* and press down. The front of the board, called the *nose*, lifts up. The back wheels act like the middle of a seesaw. Pressing one end lifts the other end.
This small change opened up new moves. Riders could lift the nose to turn sharply or to get up a curb. Kicktails became normal on boards. Later, boards got a curved-up nose too.

words.d: the back end of a skateboard that bends upward so a rider can press it
the back end of the deck
the front end of the deck

look.title: The Kicktail Patent
look.text: The patent describes a skateboard whose back end turns upward. A rider can push down on this raised end with a foot to tip the board and steer it.
look.cite: U.S. patent for a skateboard kicktail, Larry Stevenson, granted 1971 (described)

choices: the back end of the board that bends upward
check.why: A kicktail is a back end that bends up so the rider can press it.

check.q: Who got the patent for the kicktail, granted in 1971?
check.why: Larry Stevenson's kicktail patent was granted in 1971.

check.q: When a rider presses down on the tail, what happens?
check.why: Pressing the tail tips the board on the back wheels, so the nose lifts like a seesaw.

lessons.title: Try a Tail Press
lessons.mainIdea: Practice pressing the tail on grass or carpet first, with your back foot on the tail and your front foot near the front bolts.
reading: Before you start, buckle a helmet that fits snugly. Wear wrist guards, knee pads and flat shoes. Set your board on grass or carpet so it cannot roll. Have a grown-up nearby. Riding with your left foot forward is called regular. Riding with your right foot forward is called goofy. Both are normal.

First, put your front foot across the board, just behind the front *bolts*. Bolts are the four screws that hold each truck on. Next, put the ball of your back foot on the tail. Then bend your knees and keep your shoulders right over the board.

Now press the tail down slowly with your back foot. The nose rises. Let your front foot ride up gently. Then press with your front foot to set the nose back down. If the board tips you backward, you leaned back too far. Keep your weight over the middle and press softly.

words.d: the screws on top of the deck that hold the trucks on; they show where to put your feet
riding with the left foot in front
riding with the right foot in front

check.why: The ball of the back foot goes on the tail; the front foot goes behind the front bolts.

check.q: If the board tips you backward during a tail press, what is the fix?
choices: Keep your weight over the middle and press softly.
check.why: Tipping back means you leaned too far back; keep your shoulders over the board and press gently.

lessons.title: Smooth Spinning Bearings
lessons.mainIdea: In the mid-1970s, sealed precision bearings let wheels spin smoothly and kept dirt out.
reading: Inside each wheel is a *bearing*. A bearing is a ring of small steel balls between two metal rings. The wheel spins around the balls instead of rubbing straight on the axle. That means less friction and a smoother roll.

Early wheels had loose balls packed in by hand. Dirt and sand got in easily. The balls could fall out. In the mid-1970s, *sealed precision bearings* came to skateboarding. Each one was made with care and closed in by a cover.

The cover kept out dirt. The careful making kept the balls lined up. Wheels spun longer and more smoothly. Bearings are often marked with an ABEC number. That number tells how exactly a bearing was made. It is not a speed rating.

words.d: a ring of small balls inside a wheel that lets it spin smoothly around the axle
carefully made bearings with a cover that keeps dirt out; used on skateboards from the mid-1970s
the metal rod on the truck that a wheel spins around

look.title: Spin Test

check.q: What is a bearing?
choices: a ring of small balls that lets a wheel spin smoothly
the screw that holds a truck
the soft part of a wheel
check.why: A bearing is a ring of small steel balls that lets a wheel spin around the axle.

check.q: What did the cover on a sealed bearing do?
check.why: The cover sealed the bearing so dirt and sand stayed out.

check.q: What does a bearing's ABEC number tell you?
choices: how exactly the bearing was made
the top speed of the board
check.why: ABEC is a standard for how exactly a bearing is made, not a speed rating.

lessons.title: Surf Style from Dogtown
lessons.mainIdea: The Zephyr team from Santa Monica and Venice, California, skated low and fast, copying surfers.
reading: In the early 1970s, a surf shop called Zephyr stood near the beach in Santa Monica, California. The area of Santa Monica and Venice around it was nicknamed *Dogtown*. The shop had a surf team, and then a skate team.

The *Zephyr team* included Peggy Oki, Tony Alva, Jay Adams and Stacy Peralta. They surfed in the morning and skated after. They rode their boards the way they rode waves. They crouched low, swung their arms and dragged a hand on the ground in turns.
Peggy Oki was the only girl on the team. She skated in the same low, strong style as the others. Several team members became famous. Stacy Peralta later helped start the Powell Peralta company.

words.d: a skate team from a Santa Monica surf shop, known for its low, surf-style riding in the 1970s
a nickname for the part of Santa Monica and Venice, California, where the Zephyr team skated

lessons.title: Del Mar, 1975
lessons.mainIdea: At the 1975 Del Mar Nationals, the Zephyr team's low surf style surprised the crowd and changed contest skating.
reading: In 1975, a big contest called the *Del Mar Nationals* was held in Del Mar, California. Skaters came from many places. Most freestyle riders did neat tricks standing up tall, like spins and handstands.

Then the Zephyr team rode. They crouched low and carved fast, sharp turns. They touched the ground with their hands. Their style looked like surfing on concrete. Many people at the contest had never seen anything like it.

After Del Mar, magazines wrote about the Zephyr skaters. Other riders began to copy their low, aggressive *style*. Skating started to look less like dance and more like surfing. That style would soon move into empty pools.

words.d: a 1975 skateboard contest in Del Mar, California, where the Zephyr team became famous
the way a skater rides and moves on the board

lessons.title: A Dry California
lessons.mainIdea: During the California drought of 1976 to 1977, many backyard swimming pools sat empty, and skaters rode them.
reading: In 1976 and 1977, California had a *drought*. A drought is a long time with very little rain. Water was scarce, and people were asked to save it. Many backyard swimming pools were drained or left empty.
Skaters saw something special in those empty pools. The walls of a pool curve smoothly up from the floor. On urethane wheels, skaters could ride up those curves like riding up a wave.

Some skaters went into empty pools without asking the owners. That was trespassing, which means going on private property without permission. Today, skaters ride curved walls built for them at skateparks.

words.d: a long time with very little rain, when water is scarce
going onto someone else's property without permission

check.why: The drought that emptied many pools was in 1976 and 1977.

lessons.title: Riding the Curved Wall
lessons.mainIdea: Rolling up a curved wall turns motion energy into stored energy, and rolling back down turns it back into motion.
reading: The curve where a floor bends up into a wall is called *transition*. Skaters call it tranny for short. A skater rolls fast across the flat bottom and up the transition. As the skater goes higher, the board slows down.

At the highest point, the skater stops for an instant. Then gravity pulls the skater back down, and the board speeds up again. Going up, *motion energy* changes into *stored energy*. Coming down, stored energy changes back into motion energy.
Each trip loses a little energy to friction and air. So skaters bend and straighten their legs at the right moments to keep going. This is called pumping. It is like pumping on a swing.

words.d: the curved part where a flat floor bends up into a wall
the energy a thing has because it is moving
energy a thing has because of where it is, such as high up on a wall
bending and straightening the legs on a curved wall to gain speed

look.prompt: Where in the bowl is the marble moving fastest? Where does it have the most stored energy?

check.q: What is transition?
choices: the top edge of a wall

check.why: Transition is the curve where the floor bends up into the wall.

check.q: As a skater rolls up a curved wall, what happens to the board's speed?
check.why: Going up, motion energy changes into stored energy, so the board slows down.

check.q: What do skaters do to keep going back and forth on a curved wall?

check.why: Pumping adds energy to make up for what friction and air take away.

lessons.title: The First Skateparks
lessons.mainIdea: In 1976, Carlsbad Skatepark in California and Skateboard City in Florida opened as two of the first skateparks.
reading: Skaters needed places where they were welcome. In 1976, two of the first *skateparks* opened. One was Carlsbad Skatepark in Carlsbad, California. The other was Skateboard City in Port Orange, Florida.

These parks had smooth concrete runs, bowls and curved walls. Many parks charged a fee to ride. They did not have to sneak into backyard pools. Builders shaped the concrete to copy the curves skaters loved.

Many more parks opened in the late 1970s. The second boom was in full swing. Better wheels, kicktails, smooth bearings and new parks all worked together. Skateboarding had come back bigger than before.

a rounded, pool-shaped area in a skatepark with curved walls all around
